menelaus.name: Menelaus of Alexandria
menelaus.role: Alexandrian Geometer & Astronomer; Author of Sphaerica
menelaus.bio: Greco-Roman mathematician and astronomer born in Alexandria and active at Rome (where Ptolemy records two lunar occultation observations made by Menelaus in the first year of Emperor Trajan, 98 CE, Almagest VII.3). In his Sphaerica (three books), Menelaus emancipated spherical geometry from the purely stereometric circle-on-sphere treatises of Autolycus and Theodosius, defining the intrinsic spherical triangle (Book I), establishing rising-time arc inequalities (Book II), and founding spherical trigonometry upon the six-quantity Spherical Transversal Theorem (Book III.1).
works: Sphaerica (Libri III — extant in Arabic, Hebrew, and Latin)
Chords in a Circle (6 books — lost, attested by Theon of Alexandria)
Elements of Geometry (3 books — lost, attested in Arabic bibliographies)

ptolemy.name: Claudius Ptolemy
ptolemy.bio: Author of the Syntaxis Mathematica (Almagest), Planetary Hypotheses, Planisphaerium, and Geography. In Almagest I.13 (Heiberg pp. 68–76), Ptolemy preserves the oldest surviving Greek demonstration of the Planar and Spherical Menelaus Lemmas in chords of double arcs, deploying them throughout Books I–II as the sole trigonometric engine of ancient mathematical astronomy, and cites Menelaus's 98 CE Roman astronomical observations in Almagest VII.3.

euclid.name: Euclid of Alexandria
euclid.bio: Author of the Elements and Phaenomena. Menelaus explicitly models Book I of the Sphaerica as the intrinsic spherical counterpart of Euclid's Elements Book I—replacing straight lines with minor arcs of great circles, preserving SAS/SSS/ASA congruence and side-angle inequalities while overturning Euclid I.32 (angle sum = 2 right angles -> > 2 right angles in Sphaerica I.11) and establishing AAA congruence (Sphaerica I.17).

theodosius.name: Theodosius of Bithynia
theodosius.bio: Author of an earlier three-book Sphaerica treating great and parallel circles on a sphere by Euclidean solid geometry without ever defining a spherical triangle or computing trigonometric chord ratios. In Book II of Menelaus's Sphaerica (as Halley notes on pp. 75–76), single propositions of Menelaus (such as II.10) supersede and generalize multiple propositions of Theodosius Book III.

hipparchus.name: Hipparchus of Nicaea
hipparchus.role: Greek Astronomer & Pioneer of Chord Tables
hipparchus.bio: Compiled a twelve-book treatise on chords in a circle (attested by Theon of Alexandria alongside Menelaus's six-book chord treatise) and discovered the precession of the equinoxes. His chord methods prepared the ground for Menelaus's deductive axiomatization of spherical trigonometry.
works: On Chords in a Circle (12 books — lost)

pappus.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus.bio: Author of the Synagoge (Mathematical Collection). In Book VI of the Synagoge, Pappus comments directly on Menelaus's Sphaerica (calling him Menelaos ho Alexandreus) and rising-time arcs; in Book VII, Pappus proves projective cross-ratio invariance and collinearity lemmas closely allied to Menelaus's spherical cross-ratio theorem (Sphaerica III.8).

theon.name: Theon of Alexandria
theon.bio: Commentator on Ptolemy's Almagest I.13 who proved the remaining case variations of the Planar and Spherical Menelaus Theorem (including external transversal configurations noted by Halley 1758 pp. 84–85) and attested Menelaus's six-book treatise on chords.

proclus.name: Proclus Diadochus
proclus.role: Neoplatonic Philosopher & Commentator on Euclid Book I
proclus.bio: In his Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements (Friedlein p. 345), Proclus preserves an alternative direct proof by Menelaus of Euclid I.25 (avoiding reductio ad absurdum), confirming Menelaus's lifelong preoccupation with direct, intrinsic proofs free of indirect case-splitting.
works: Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements

ishaq-ibn-hunayn.name: Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn
ishaq-ibn-hunayn.role: Baghdad Translator of Greek Mathematical Classics into Arabic
ishaq-ibn-hunayn.bio: Son of Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq in Abbasid Baghdad, renowned translator of Euclid's Elements, Ptolemy's Almagest, and Menelaus's Sphaerica from Greek into Arabic (attested in the Bodleian Hebrew colophon cited by Costard 1758 p. iv: ex Versione R. Isaaci Filii Honaini).
works: Arabic Translation of Euclid's Elements (revised by Thābit ibn Qurra)

thabit-ibn-qurra.name: Thābit ibn Qurra
thabit-ibn-qurra.bio: Composed an influential Arabic treatise on the Sector Figure (Risāla fī al-Shakl al-Qaṭṭāʿ), exhaustively classifying all eighteen combinatorially valid cases of Menelaus's compound-ratio theorem and transmitting it to Latin Europe as Figura Kata / Figura Alchata.
works: Kitāb fī al-Shakl al-Qaṭṭāʿ (On the Sector Figure)

abu-nasr-mansur.name: Abū Naṣr Manṣūr ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿIrāq
abu-nasr-mansur.role: Khwarazmian Geometer, Teacher of al-Bīrūnī & Redactor of Menelaus
abu-nasr-mansur.bio: Completed in 1007–1008 CE the definitive medieval Arabic critical redaction of Menelaus's Sphaerica, replacing Greek chords of double arcs with explicit sines (jayb) while scrupulously preserving Menelaus's geometric architecture, and co-discovering the autonomous Spherical Law of Sines.
works: Kitāb Mānalāwus fī al-Ukar (Redaction of Menelaus's Sphaerica)

gerard-of-cremona.name: Gerard of Cremona
gerard-of-cremona.role: Toledan Translator of Arabic Science into Latin
gerard-of-cremona.bio: Translated Ptolemy's Almagest and an Arabic redaction of Menelaus's Sphaerica (Liber Menelai de Sphaericis) into Latin at Toledo in the twelfth century, introducing Menelaus's spherical geometry to Campanus, Jordanus, Fibonacci, and Simon Bredon.

jacob-ben-machir.name: Jacob ben Machir ibn Tibbon (Prophatius Judaeus)
jacob-ben-machir.bio: Translated Menelaus's Sphaerica from Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn's Arabic lineage into Hebrew at Montpellier in the late thirteenth century—the exact Hebrew manuscript witness in the Bodleian Huntington collection collated by Edmond Halley (Costard 1758 p. iv; Halley Scholion p. 82).
works: Sefer Menelaus ba-Temunot ha-Kaduriyot (Hebrew translation of Sphaerica)

maurolico.name: Francesco Maurolico (Franciscus Maurolycus)
maurolico.role: Sicilian Benedictine Mathematician & First Printed Editor of Menelaus
maurolico.bio: Published at Messina in 1558 the editio princeps of Menelaus's Sphaerica alongside Theodosius, freely restructuring proofs and interpolating Renaissance trigonometric corollaries while recognizing Menelaus's treatise (in his 1543 letter to Cardinal Bembo) as the fountainhead whence 'the whole science of spherical triangles flows'.

mersenne.name: Marin Mersenne
mersenne.bio: Included an abridged Latin synopsis of Menelaus's Sphaerica (under the medieval corrupted name Mileus) inside his Universae Geometriae Mixtaeque Mathematicae Synopsis (Paris, 1644), heavily dependent on Maurolico's 1558 recension.

halley.name: Edmond Halley
halley.role: Savilian Professor of Geometry at Oxford, Astronomer Royal & Editor of Menelaus
halley.bio: After editing Apollonius's De Sectione Rationis (1706) from Arabic and Conica (1710), Halley collated Bodleian Hebrew (Huntington) and Arabic manuscripts to establish the first philologically faithful Latin edition of Menelaus's Sphaerica, engraving its plates and printing sheets pp. 1–112 at Oxford before his death; published posthumously in 1758 with a preface by George Costard.
works: Menelai Sphaericorum Libri III (Oxford, printed c. 1712–1741, issued 1758)

costard.name: George Costard
costard.role: Oxford Orientalist, Historian of Astronomy & Author of the 1758 Preface
costard.bio: Fellow of Wadham College, Oxford, who authored the eight-page Latin scholarly preface (Benevolo Lectori, pp. [i]–[viii]) bringing Halley's long-printed sheets of Menelaus's Sphaerica before the public in 1758, documenting the Bodleian Huntington manuscripts and ancient Greek witnesses.
works: Praefatio ad Menelai Sphaericorum Libros III (Oxford, 1758)

ceva.name: Giovanni Ceva
ceva.role: Italian Geometer; Discoverer of Ceva's Concurrency Theorem
ceva.bio: Published De lineis rectis se invicem secantibus statica constructio (Milan, 1678), both rediscovering Planar Menelaus via statics/centers of gravity and proving its exact projective point-line dual—Ceva's Theorem on concurrent cevians (+1 signed ratio product vs. Menelaus's -1).
works: De lineis rectis se invicem secantibus statica constructio (1678)

carnot.name: Lazare Carnot
carnot.role: French Geometer; Pioneer of Modern Projective Transversal Theory
carnot.bio: In his Géométrie de position (1803) and Essai sur la théorie des transversales (1806), Carnot placed Menelaus's Transversal Theorem at the center of modern synthetic projective geometry, generalizing it to algebraic curves of arbitrary degree (Carnot's Theorem) and signed segment ratios.
works: Essai sur la théorie des transversales (1806)

poncelet.name: Jean-Victor Poncelet
poncelet.role: French Mathematician; Co-Founder of Projective Geometry
poncelet.bio: In his Traité des propriétés projectives des figures (1822), Poncelet elevated Menelaus's Theorem, harmonic cross-ratios, and pole-polar duality into universal projective principles uniting Desargues, Pascal, Monge, and Ceva.
works: Traité des propriétés projectives des figures (1822)

bjornbo.name: Axel Anthon Björnbo
bjornbo.role: Danish Historian of Mathematics & Philologist of Menelaus
bjornbo.bio: Student of Heiberg and Zeuthen whose landmark Teubner monograph Studien über Menelaos' Sphärik (1902) systematically reconstructed the proposition numbering, terminology, and textual stemma of Menelaus's Sphaerica across Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, and Latin witnesses.

heiberg.name: Johan Ludvig Heiberg
heiberg.role: Danish Classical Philologist & Critical Editor of Euclid and Ptolemy
heiberg.bio: Edited the authoritative Teubner Greek critical editions of Euclid's Elements (1883–1888) and Ptolemy's Syntaxis Mathematica (1898–1903), establishing the polytonic Greek text of the Menelaus Lemmas in Almagest I.13.
